One of the most fucked up benchmarks: wastes your time and doesn't show you a clear results table.

Better benchmarks:

  • https://tfb-status.techempower.com

  • https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks

  • https://github.com/drujensen/fib

What benchmarks don't show you is that 99% of the time performance doesn't matter. If the results are cached (as they should be), output generated by hand-optimized assembly and some high-level scripting language will be the same. Also all languages wait for IP (disk, networking, etc) at the same speed. You're probably using a library or a server written in C/C++ (Nginx, PostgreSQL, JSON, etc) no matter which language you use. So the vast majority of the time using the most productive language is far more important than using the fastest one.

For that 1% of the time when something needs to be optimized for performance, you can hire someone to rewrite something that already works in C/C++. Not everyone needs to be a super-experienced C/C++ optimization specialist - division of labor - for most programmers understanding the business logic is far more important.

If you do want improved performance but without investing in an optimization specialist, then it's a tradeoff between effort and performance. Languages like Rust, Nim, D, Ada, Cython, Crystal, etc come close to C/C++ performance with additional safety and readability benefits. If you do 99% of your programming in Python, then Nim or Cython are reasonable optimization choices; if you script in Ruby, you'll probably prefer Crystal; etc.

JVM, DotNet, and functional languages are rarely a good choice - they're neither good for productivity nor performance. Their scores on the performance benchmarks are usually higher than in the real world, where RAM can be a bottleneck (ex busy Web application server or mobile). Languages like Nim and D are both faster, more RAM-efficient, and more productive than C#, Java, Go, Scala, Haskell, Ocaml, etc.
